 Permanent daylight saving time would push High Country winter sunrises past 8 a.m.

 HIGH COUNTRY — On Nov. 1, most clocks throughout the nation will fall back an hour from 2 a.m. to 1 a.m. Daylight saving time adjusts the time of day by one hour to match winter’s short, dark days and summer’s long, bright days. The clock change makes it seem like the sun rises one hour earlier in winter and one hour later in summer, without any natural change in day length.
 While most Americans — outside Arizona and Hawaii — will change their clocks on Nov. 1, ending the twice-yearly clock changes is under discussion.
 Congress is working on a new law, the Sunshine Protection Act, that would end the clock changes in November and March by making daylight saving time permanent. The House passed the bill 308-117 on July 14, but the Senate has not passed it. President Donald Trump has backed making daylight saving time permanent, and the White House urged lawmakers to support the bill ahead of the House vote. The bill is currently before the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
 This is not the first time that changes to daylight saving time have been proposed in Congress. According to Congress.gov , the system of having different parts of the country run on different times began in 1883, when railroads adopted standard time zones to reduce confusion in rail travel. Four time zones were established, and local communities largely followed the time zones the railroads adopted.
 Congress first set time zones and daylight saving time in 1918 with the Standard Time Act, or Calder Act. The STA established five standard time zones: Eastern, Central, Mountain, Pacific and Alaskan. The act authorized the Interstate Commerce Commission to change the zone boundaries as it deemed necessary.
 “After World War I, Congress abolished summer DST at the federal level, although it remained a local option, with some states continuing to observe it,” according to Congress.gov . “With a few exceptions, this patchwork of local DST observance continued into the 1960s when the ICC recommended that Congress reexamine the issue.”
 Reexamination came in the form of the Uniform Time Act of 1966.
 “The (Uniform Time) Act mandated standard time within the established time zones and specified the observance period for DST: Clocks would be advanced one hour beginning at 2 a.m. on the last Sunday in April and turned back one hour at 2:00 a.m. on the last Sunday in October,” according to Congress.gov . “States were allowed to exempt themselves from DST as long as the entire state did so. In 1972, the Uniform Time Act was amended to also allow states that were split between time zones to exempt from DST that part of the state lying within a different time zone.”
 Since 2007, clocks have moved forward on the second Sunday in March and back on the first Sunday in November.
 According to an October article in USA Today titled “Are clocks falling back this weekend? Here’s what to know,” permanent daylight saving time would leave the country in darkness longer during winter mornings. Sleep experts, including the American Academy of Sleep Medicine, favor permanent standard time instead, saying it better matches the body’s internal clock. In addition to health impacts, according to Congress.gov , changes to daylight saving time could affect the economy, outdoor recreation, and energy savings.
 According to the same USA Today article, supporters of ending the clock changes cite the annoyance of changing clocks twice a year. A March 2023 YouGov survey found 62% of Americans favored ending the time changes. A January 2025 Gallup poll found that 54% opposed daylight saving time. But that poll also found that, given the choice, 48% preferred permanent standard time, 24% preferred permanent daylight saving time and 19% wanted to keep switching.
 Under the bill, residents would stop changing clocks, and winter sunrises and sunsets would come an hour later; summer times would not change.
 Here is how sunrise and sunset times compare under the current system, permanent daylight saving time (the Sunshine Protection Act) and permanent standard time.
 Dec. 1: current system and permanent standard time
 Ashe County: sunrise at 7:19 a.m., sunset at 5:10 p.m.
 Avery County: sunrise at 7:20 a.m., sunset at 5:13 p.m.
 Watauga County: sunrise at 7:19 a.m., sunset at 5:11 p.m.
 Dec. 1: permanent daylight saving time
 Ashe County: sunrise at 8:19 a.m., sunset at 6:10 p.m.
 Avery County: sunrise at 8:20 a.m., sunset at 6:13 p.m.
 Watauga County: sunrise at 8:19 a.m., sunset at 6:11 p.m.
 July 1: current system and permanent daylight saving time
 Ashe County: sunrise at 6:11 a.m., sunset at 8:48 p.m.
 Avery County: sunrise at 6:14 a.m., sunset at 8:48 p.m.
 Watauga County: sunrise at 6:13 a.m., sunset at 8:48 p.m.
 July 1: permanent standard time
 Ashe County: sunrise at 5:11 a.m., sunset at 7:48 p.m.
 Avery County: sunrise at 5:14 a.m., sunset at 7:48 p.m.
 Watauga County: sunrise at 5:13 a.m., sunset at 7:48 p.m.
 Sunrise and sunset times are from Sunrise-Sunset.org , which calculates them using a solar position formula published by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
